title: What Might Be the Master Algorithm for Intelligent Machine?
content: Since Turing, a line of researchers has asked whether one principle could account for intelligence in general: Solomonoff’s universal induction, Newell and Simon’s physical symbol system, Hutter’s AIXI and the Legg–Hutter definition of universal intelligence, Schmidhuber’s Gödel machine, Friston’s free-energy principle, Domingos’ Master Algorithm, Sutton and Silver’s reward-is-enough and era-of-experience theses, LeCun’s autonomous machine intelligence, Hawkins’ thousand brains, Kauffman’s adjacent possible, Levin’s multi-scale competency, and the no-free-lunch theorems that say no single optimiser can win everywhere. This paper maps that landscape, sorts the proposals into six scenarios and twelve hypothesis families, asks of each where its space of possibilities comes from, and derives fifty requirements a Master Algorithm must meet in an open world where the state is partial, the action space incomplete, and the agent’s own actions change what is possible next. The requirements reduce to seven irreducible functions applied at five levels. Against that framework we test the five theses of the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence (AFI) as one candidate: they hold as a vocabulary and as pre-choice readouts and stand short of a mechanism at the two stages that create possibilities and learning rules. The Freedom hypothesis, written in full as Freedom(x) = (Perception(x)/Distortion(x))α∞, is graded layer by layer. The same six primitives survive bacterium, plant, salamander, human, swarm and AI. We treat the universe itself as an instrument — adjudicator, computer, store, constraint and source of the adjacent possible — and swarm intelligence as the stress test where averaging, data volume and consensus each leave better collective perception unguaranteed. We specify an executable fifteen-component machine, a released procedural world (Riverlands) with seven pre-registered predictions, thirty counterfactuals and twelve falsifiers. The paper establishes a requirements framework, a candidate architecture and decisive experiments, and leaves AFI’s status as a Master Algorithm an open question.
